messages.content: Write a customer case study about a company that adopted a continuous delivery platform and now deploys more often. Around 250 words.

**Vantis Freight stopped releasing on Saturdays**

Vantis Freight brokers truckload capacity for regional grocery distributors. Through 2023 its engineers worked to a six-week release train, and every release landed on a Saturday: a dozen people on a bridge call, a two-hour freeze, and a rollback plan last rehearsed in March.

"The writing was never the bottleneck," says Priya Ranganathan, VP of Engineering. "The last mile cost us a weekend, every time."

They began in February 2024 with one service, the rate-quoting API, the thing that broke most. Pipeline templates took the place of roughly 4,000 lines of hand-written Jenkins Groovy. Progressive rollout took over what had been a person watching a Grafana dashboard with a coffee.

Month one went badly. Two services moved without trouble. The third, a Rails monolith carrying a 40-minute test suite, had to be broken apart before any of it got faster, and that took ten weeks that nobody had budgeted for.

Fourteen months on, across 23 services:

- Deploys: 8 a quarter to 11 a day (median)
- Merge to production: six weeks to 34 minutes
- Change failure rate: 19% to 4.2%
- Rollback: automatic, 90 seconds median

No more Saturdays. No more bridge call.

"People quote the deploy count back at me," Ranganathan says. "What I care about is that we stopped batching risk. A bad deploy now means looking at four commits instead of four hundred."

Nine services remain on the old path. They move in Q3.

Vantis Freight matches truckload capacity with regional grocery distributors. Until 2023 its engineers shipped on a six-week train, and each release fell on a Saturday: twelve people on a bridge call, a two-hour freeze, and a rollback plan nobody had practiced since March.

"Writing the code was never what slowed us down," says Priya Ranganathan, VP of Engineering. "The last mile ate a weekend every time."

They started in February 2024 with the rate-quoting API, the service that broke most often. Pipeline templates replaced about 4,000 lines of hand-rolled Jenkins Groovy. Progressive rollout replaced a person watching a Grafana dashboard with a coffee.

The first month was rough. Two services moved cleanly. The third, a Rails monolith with a 40-minute test suite, had to be split apart before anything got faster, and the split took ten weeks nobody had planned for.

Fourteen months later, across 23 services:

- Deploys: 8 per quarter to 11 per day (median)
- Merge to production: six weeks to 34 minutes
- Change failure rate: 19% to 4.2%
- Rollback: automatic, 90-second median

The Saturdays are gone. So is the bridge call.

"Everyone repeats the deploy number back to me," Ranganathan says. "The part I care about is that we quit batching risk. A bad deploy means reading four commits now, not four hundred."

Nine services still run the old path. Those move in Q3.
